In addition to these shortcomings, their rather simple 1-step photoswitching mechanism involving a single reaction coordinate (e.g. photoisomerization or electrocyclization) and picosecond (or faster) time scales inherently hinders the design and development of novel candidates that are based on similar photoreactive moieties. The next generation of molecular photoswitches could benefit greatly from more complex multistep mechanisms with tunable intermediates that can be exploited to target a range of desired functionality (Figure 1b). Donor-Acceptor Stenhouse Adducts15-19 (DASAs) are a novel class of photoswitches that incorporate complexity by introducing tunable structural features in the form of donor and acceptor groups linked together via a hydroxylated triene bridge that can be systematically altered to influence their multistep photoswitching behavior (Figure 1b). These switches display a rich and complex multistep mechanism consisting of photoisomerization, 4-electrocyclization, and proton transfer (PT) processes20-26 (Figure 1b). This complexity, in contrast to previous single reaction coordinate molecular photoswitches, improves the ability to tailor the chromophores to a range of practical applications (e.g. smart materials,27-31 photopharmacology,9,32-36 nano systems,37-39 and receptors40-42). Exploiting the properties of these promising molecules to design purposed photosensitive materials ultimately hinges upon the ability to understand and control their stepwise dynamics at the molecular level. Several experimental and theoretical studies have been performed to unravel the DASA switching mechanism, but key intermediates and their interconnecting 2 LLNL-JRNL-822958 pathways have yet to be fully characterized. For example, rapid scan infrared (IR) and transient absorption spectroscopy identified the open/closed forms (reactant and products) of the complete reaction20-26 (Figure 1b), but these techniques are quite limited when identifying short-lived intermediates with similar structure and electronic properties. Additionally, traditional hypothesis- driven computational approaches have been employed43-45 to propose possible reaction mechanisms based on the characterization of stationary points and pathways connecting them. Unfortunately, photoinduced processes often do not follow equilibrium dynamics and it is unlikely that a single reaction pathway is sufficient to describe the inherent dynamical behavior in multistage chromophores like DASA. In this contribution, we reveal the complex switching mechanisms of Meldrum’s acid 1st generation DASA by direct simulation of the molecular dynamics after photoexcitation, including long time evolution on the ground state to identify both excited state and ground state mechanisms and a plethora of final products. Our approach is an in silico mimic of a photochemical experiment, without any perturbation to the molecular dynamics. Because of the complex ground state chemistry after internal conversion, this requires ≈2 ns of AIMD (for a chromophore with almost 50 atoms) including multiple electronic states and surface crossing effects. Our approach is hypothesis-free and represents a discovery-based computational approach to photochemistry. Computational expense has been an obstacle to this type of discovery approach to photochemistry, especially in cases where modeling of subsequent reactions on the “hot” ground state is required.
